editorial.headline: Electronic Design: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This industrial-design activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s PMA moratorium blocks its registration there today.
editorial.body:
**The Bali conclusion comes first:** a foreign investor cannot register this activity through a PMA company in Bali today. That is not a judgment on the design work itself or on its national investment status. At the Large scale, OSS classifies every scope in the activity as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, resulting in the recorded Bali status of being blocked by risk class. The restriction is tied to a Governor’s letter and is recorded as applying from May 2026. For a founder considering a Bali vehicle, that practical registration outcome needs to lead the discussion.

This is an industrial-design activity focused on developing products that carry, process, store, power and control electronic functions. Its scope includes design for information-technology products, communication and control equipment, sound- or image-recording products, data-storage products, power-generation and motor-drive products, power-storage and power-amplification products, and products for electricity distribution and control. It also covers the design of cooling machinery, washing machines, and drying and cleaning machines. The record adds an important working detail: this design activity is also undertaken through specialised software. In plain terms, the classification concerns the product-design layer—the development of a design solution for equipment—rather than a generic label for the wider electronics economy.

Registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales. That breadth makes the activity relevant to a range of design practices, from compact studios to substantial product-development organisations. Scale is not merely background in the Bali assessment, however. The record explicitly places the risk finding at the Besar scale, where every listed scope is Low or Medium-Low. It is a reason to read the activity’s scope and local PMA treatment together, rather than treating national openness as a local registration clearance.

Nationally, the position is open: foreign ownership may reach 100%, under the cited Presidential Regulations. That national ceiling is clear, and it should not be quietly recast as a Bali permission. Bali’s restriction rests on the recorded risk classification and the provincial PMA moratorium, not on a lower stated foreign-ownership ceiling. The result is a precise distinction: the activity remains nationally open to PMA at full foreign ownership; for PMA registration in Bali, the recorded moratorium blocks it.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness to full foreign ownership is not a Bali registration clearance.
